title: Staff health checks, immunity records and staying away when unwell
audience: Cleaners and service workers who enter care areas, including dental and aged care settings.
learningOutcomes: Explain why staff health checks protect patients and colleagues.
State when to report an illness and stay away from care areas.
Name the records a care-area worker should keep and show.

instruction.heading: Why staff health is part of infection control
instruction.body: Workers can catch infections at work and can pass them to patients, colleagues and residents. A staff health programme therefore covers the start of employment, ongoing training, immunity records and the decision to stay away when unwell. Health checks happen when someone is hired and again when their duties change significantly. A new worker should not start in a care area until the checks are complete and they are cleared to work.

instruction.heading: Training and your part in it
instruction.body: Infection control training is expected at induction and then kept current through evidence of further education. The training covers occupational hazards such as bloodborne infections and tuberculosis. Your part is to attend, keep your own training records, and tell your employer when a training record is due.

instruction.heading: Immunity and vaccination
instruction.body: Staff who may handle blood, other body fluids or sharps are expected to be protected against hepatitis B, and the source sets out a testing approach for people whose immune response to the vaccine is weak. The source also encourages staff without immunity to some other diseases to consider vaccination. The schedules are not copied into this lesson.

instruction.heading: Staying away when unwell
instruction.body: Staff with symptoms that may come from an infection should report them, and should not attend work while they are likely to pass the infection on. The source names categories such as chest and airway infections, stomach bugs, eye infections, weeping skin sores when the worker would touch patients or food, chickenpox, and shingles where the rash could reach patients. You do not diagnose yourself. You tell your supervisor before the shift where you can, and the site's staff illness policy decides when you return.

procedure: Complete the pre-employment health checks before your first shift in a care area.
Keep a copy of your immunity and training records, and tell your employer when a record is due.
Report any symptom covered by the site's staff illness policy to your supervisor before your shift starts.
Do not return to care-area work until your employer has cleared you under that policy.
Cover any infected skin lesion and tell your supervisor before you touch patients, food or patient equipment.
Record the report, its date and the decision taken.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner wakes with a sore throat and a fever on a day they are rostered in a residential aged care facility.
workedExamples.reasoning: Report the symptoms to the supervisor before the shift and follow the staff illness policy. Do not work in resident areas while unwell, and do not take medicine to mask the symptoms and attend anyway.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner has an open rash on one hand and is asked to clean a room where patients receive dialysis.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cleaner take the task?
workedExamples.reasoning: Cover the lesion, report it, and let the supervisor decide under the site's skin policy whether the rash allows the task. The cleaner does not decide alone.

equipmentAndPpe: Training and immunity records held by the worker and the employer
Waterproof dressing for any broken skin

commonErrors.error: Working while unwell because the shift is short.
commonErrors.prevention: Report before the shift and follow the staff illness policy.

commonErrors.error: Assuming immunity is on record because a vaccination was given years ago.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the records and ask the employer what the current requirement is.

commonErrors.error: Covering the symptoms with medicine and going in anyway.
commonErrors.prevention: Report the symptoms. Treatment decisions go to a doctor, and return to work is decided under site policy.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson gives no medical advice. Diagnosis and treatment of a worker's own illness belong to their doctor.
The employer and the state health authority decide what applies.
Health information is confidential and is shared only with the people who need it to make a work decision.

qualityStandard: Pre-employment checks are complete before the first care-area shift.
Illness is reported before the shift wherever the worker is able to do so.
documentationEvidence: Pre-employment health check record held by the employer
Immunity record kept by the worker and held by the employer
Illness report with its date and the decision on return
summary: Staff health is an infection control measure, and the employer runs the programme.
Report illness and infected skin before the shift, and follow the site's policy.

knowledgeChecks.question: You wake with a fever and a cough on a day you are rostered to a ward. What is the first step?
options: Go in and wear a mask and keep working as normal for the whole long shift today
Tell your supervisor before the shift and follow the staff illness policy about staying away.
Work only in the car park with the windows wound down and the radio on loudly
Take extra medicine and attend and then go straight to the wards without a mask

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are immunity records kept for workers who may touch blood or sharps?
options: To confirm the worker's protection against infections they could catch or pass on.
To rank staff by speed and to compare them with the other staff in the ward
To set wage levels and to decide which staff get the best shifts each week
Records are not needed for the staff who work only in the office and the car park

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has an infected skin lesion on the arm. What applies?
options: Cover it, report it, and follow the site's rule before touching patients, food or patient equipment.
Keep working if it does not hurt, and cover it later and tell the patient about it at the end of the shift
Hide it under the uniform and keep working in all areas and tell nobody about it at all
Clean it with a patient's wipe and then wipe the patient's bed rails and the bedside table
